claims.text: Premelting onset in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential migration of Cu atoms to the surface.
Surface-segregated Cu creates a Cu-rich, disordered liquid-like layer.
The Cu-rich surface layer nucleates melting and allows it to propagate into the nanoparticle core.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are crystalline and have a uniform elemental distribution.
The proposed experiment combines in situ high-resolution TEM, EDS line scans, and in situ X-ray diffraction during heating.
Heating is conducted in inert argon at approximately 5 °C/min from room temperature to 900–1300 °C.
An inert atmosphere and slow heating ramp will ensure that oxidation and external contamination are minimal.
A Cu-rich surface region is the structural mediator and serves as the nucleation site for premelting.
Heterogeneous atomic mobility causes Cu to diffuse preferentially to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu has a lower melting point and weaker bonding than the other relevant constituents, promoting local surface disorder.
Once formed, the disordered Cu-rich surface layer destabilizes the crystalline core and drives inward melting progression.
Premelting will first appear locally at the nanoparticle surface as a Cu-enriched disordered phase at a lower temperature than uniform melting.
Surface premelting will be followed by progressive melting of the nanoparticle core.
The comparison baseline is homogeneous elemental distribution with uniform melting onset and no premelting surface segregation.
Nanoparticle size and minor compositional fluctuations may change the temperature at which premelting begins.
EDS line scans can be used to measure spatial concentration profiles across the nanoparticles.
X-ray diffraction can monitor loss of crystalline order during the transition.
Absence of significant surface Cu enrichment, or spatially uniform melting without a Cu-rich disordered layer, would falsify the hypothesis.
